title: Engineering manager situations
authored: Project-authored reflective scenarios (2026-10-23). Not a validated situational judgment test; there are no correct answers.

scenarios.title: Underperformer 1:1
scenarios.prompt: An engineer on your team has missed several commitments this quarter. Peers have started working around them.

options.text: Name the pattern plainly in your next 1:1 and agree a concrete improvement plan.
Ask open questions first to find out what is going on before naming a problem.
Give them smaller, clearer tasks for a few weeks and see if things improve.
Bring in HR early to make sure the process is handled correctly.

scenarios.title: Split hiring panel
scenarios.prompt: Two interviewers strongly support a candidate; one strongly objects, citing how the candidate treated a junior interviewer.

options.text: Reject; a credible concern about behaviour outweighs strong skills.
Hold a debrief where each interviewer presents evidence, then decide.
Arrange one more conversation focused on collaboration.
Hire; the majority view and the skills gap on the team decide it.

scenarios.title: Conflict between two seniors
scenarios.prompt: Two senior engineers have been arguing in pull request comments for weeks. The rest of the team is getting tired of it.

options.text: Meet them together, name the impact and ask them to agree working rules.
Talk to each separately and coach them on how they come across.
Make the technical call yourself so the argument ends.
Give it time; strong engineers often argue before they converge.

scenarios.title: Reorganisation news
scenarios.prompt: You learn about an upcoming reorganisation affecting your team two weeks before it is announced. You are asked to keep it confidential.

options.text: Keep it confidential and prepare answers for the questions you expect.
Push leadership to announce earlier, explaining the cost of rumours.
Carry on as normal and deal with it when it is public.
Quietly delay decisions the reorganisation might reverse.

scenarios.title: Signs of strain
scenarios.prompt: A reliable engineer has been working late every night, has become short with colleagues and has stopped taking breaks.

options.text: Tell them what you have noticed and ask how they are doing.
Reduce their load quietly by moving work to others.
Remind the whole team about working hours and time off.
Point them to the employee support programme.

scenarios.title: Promotion case
scenarios.prompt: You believe an engineer is ready for promotion, but their impact is hard to show with the evidence the committee usually expects.

options.text: Write a strong case anyway and argue for it in the committee.
Wait a cycle and help them build visible evidence first.
Ask a respected peer manager to review the case before submitting.
Submit it and let the committee decide without lobbying.

scenarios.title: Commitment versus capacity
scenarios.prompt: Leadership asks your team to take on a new project. The team is already at full capacity.

options.text: Say yes only if something specific is dropped, and name what.
Say yes and find a way; the project matters to the company.
Ask the team how they would make room before you answer.
Present a capacity plan with options and let leadership choose.

scenarios.title: Skip-level feedback
scenarios.prompt: Your manager tells you that two of your reports said, in skip-level meetings, that they feel micromanaged.

options.text: Raise it openly with the team and ask what you should do differently.
Reflect privately and step back from details without announcing it.
Ask your manager for specifics before changing anything.
Agree explicit decision rights with each report in your next 1:1s.

scenarios.title: Blame in a postmortem
scenarios.prompt: In an incident review, a senior leader repeatedly asks 'who pushed the change?' and a junior engineer looks uncomfortable.

options.text: Interrupt and redirect to what in the system allowed the change through.
Let the meeting continue, then speak to the leader privately afterwards.
Answer the question yourself to take the attention off the junior.
Stay neutral; the leader is entitled to ask.

scenarios.title: Team across time zones
scenarios.prompt: Half of your team is eight hours ahead. The remote half says decisions get made without them.

options.text: Move decisions into written proposals with a 24-hour comment window.
Rotate meeting times so the inconvenience is shared.
Give the remote half ownership of a clear area so they decide locally.
Record meetings and send summaries; that should be enough.

scenarios.title: Tech lead wants a rewrite
scenarios.prompt: Your respected tech lead proposes a six-month rewrite of the core service. Product leadership is sceptical.

options.text: Back the tech lead publicly and make the case to product leadership.
Ask for an incremental plan that delivers value every month.
Commission a short spike to test the riskiest assumption first.
Side with product leadership; six months is too long to justify now.

scenarios.title: Top performer may leave
scenarios.prompt: You hear that your strongest engineer is interviewing elsewhere.

options.text: Ask them directly and openly what would make them stay.
Wait for them to raise it; respect their privacy.
Quietly start a retention case with your manager and HR.
In your next 1:1, ask broadly about their goals and growth.
